proofs.proof_tex:
The graph-gadget definition gives \((B_G)_{ii}=0\), because \(G\) is simple and each local block has zero diagonal. Hence \((W_G)_{ii}=1\), which verifies the unit-diagonal assumption. To verify invertibility without using the later stability theorem, eliminate \(v_i,w_i\) from \((I_{3n}-B_G)x=0\). At \(z=1\), the unswitched calculation gives
\[
 \det(I_{3n}-B_G)
 =\det\!\left(\left(1-p-r\right)I_n-gA_G\right).
\]
Now
\[
 1-p-r=\frac{13}{8}+\frac{15}{16}\delta,
 \qquad \|gA_G\|_2\leq g(n-1)<1,
\]
so every eigenvalue of the displayed symmetric matrix is positive. Thus \(W_G\) is invertible.

By the hypothesis of the proposition, the coordinates of \(e\) are mutually independent, centered, continuous, non-Gaussian, and have variance one. Defining \(X=W_G^{-1}e\) gives \(W_GX=e\), so the linear-SEM assumption holds. The preceding two paragraphs verify the unit-diagonal and invertibility assumptions, and the stated properties of \(e\) verify independent errors, at most one Gaussian coordinate, and positive finite error variances. Therefore the definition of the square cyclic LiNG class gives
\[
 (P_X,W_G,e)\in\mathcal M_{3n}.
\]

Fix \(\pi\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{adm}}(W_G)\). By admissibility, every \(d_{\pi,i}=W_G[\pi(i),i]\) is nonzero, so the normalized-candidate definition makes \(T_\pi\) an invertible monomial matrix and
\[
 (T_\pi e)_i=d_{\pi,i}^{-1}e_{\pi(i)}.
\]
A permutation preserves mutual independence, and multiplication by a nonzero constant preserves centering, continuity, and non-Gaussianity. Moreover,
\[
 \operatorname{Var}((T_\pi e)_i)=d_{\pi,i}^{-2}>0
\]
is finite. Normalization gives
\[
 (W_\pi)_{ii}=d_{\pi,i}^{-1}W_G[\pi(i),i]=1,
\]
and \(W_\pi=T_\pi W_G\) is invertible. Finally,
\[
 W_\pi X=T_\pi W_GX=T_\pi e.
\]
Thus every admissible normalized assignment supplies a legal structural representation of the same observational vector \(X\), with all claimed error-law properties.

First, every intended permutation \(\pi_S\) is admissible. A fixed coordinate uses a diagonal entry equal to one, while a \(u_i\)-\(v_i\) swap uses the two nonzero entries \(W_G[v_i,u_i]=-p=25/16\) and \(W_G[u_i,v_i]=-1\). Distinct subsets give distinct permutations.

The analytic-homotopy certification theorem exhausts the spectrum of each intended assignment. If \(S\in\mathcal I(G)\), its \(3n-2|S|\) noncritical roots have modulus less than \(9/10\), and its remaining roots lie in the two critical disks and have modulus at most \(1-\delta/10\). Therefore
\[
 \rho(B_{\pi_S})\leq\max\left\{\frac9{10},1-\frac\delta{10}\right\}<1.
\]
In particular, \(S=\varnothing\) proves \(\rho(B_G)<1\). If \(S\notin\mathcal I(G)\), the same theorem supplies an eigenvalue of modulus at least \(1+g/20\), so \(\pi_S\) is not stable.

It remains only to check completeness of the orbit. The support-cycle classification in the certification theorem shows that every admissible permutation not equal to an intended \(\pi_S\) either contains a root-only cycle or contains a local \(u_i\)-\(w_i\) swap. In the first case its spectral radius is greater than \(1/(2g)>1\). In the second case, when no root-only cycle is present, it has an eigenvalue with real part greater than \(5/4\), hence with modulus greater than one. Thus every unintended admissible assignment is unstable, and
\[
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(W_G)
 =\{\pi_S:S\in\mathcal I(G)\}.
\]

The proposition on gadget-law validity shows simultaneously that the reference and every normalized assignment are legal same-law cyclic LiNG mechanisms; the spectral argument is therefore inside the declared causal model rather than merely matrix algebra. Finally, the only nonintegral entries are formed from
\[
 \varepsilon_n=\frac{1}{2^{40}(n+1)^4},\qquad
 g=\varepsilon_n^2,\qquad
 \delta=\varepsilon_n^3,\qquad
 p=-\frac{25}{16},\qquad
 r=\frac{15}{16}(1-\delta).
\]
Their numerators and denominators have \(O(\log(n+1))\) bits, and the adjacency entries are zero or one. Constructing the \(3n\)-dimensional sparse matrix takes polynomial time and preserves this per-entry bit bound. All assertions of the theorem follow.

We first prove membership in \(\#\mathrm P\) with the verifier stated in the theorem. Extend the promised function to all binary rational matrices by returning zero when the input is malformed or fails membership in \(\mathcal R_q\). Unit diagonal, rational encoding, and invertibility are decidable by exact rational arithmetic. Schur stability is also exactly decidable in polynomial time as follows.

For a rational matrix \(C\), solve the rational linear system
\[
 H-C^{\mathsf T}HC=I_q. \tag{3}
\]
If \(\rho(C)<1\), the convergent series
\[
 H=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(C^k)^{\mathsf T}C^k
\]
solves (3) and is positive definite. It is the unique solution because the homogeneous equation iterates to
\(H=(C^k)^{\mathsf T}HC^k\to0\). Conversely, if (3) has a positive-definite solution and \(Cv=\lambda v\) for a nonzero complex eigenvector, then
\[
 (1-|\lambda|^2)v^*Hv=v^*v>0,
\]
so \(|\lambda|<1\). Hence \(\rho(C)<1\). If the coefficient operator in (3) is singular, \(C\) cannot be stable, because stability gave uniqueness. Thus solving (3), checking symmetry, and applying exact positive-definiteness tests decides stability.

The system has dimension \(q^2\). Fraction-free elimination produces its unique rational solution, when it exists, with polynomially many bits by the determinant bound for an integer clearing of the denominators; exact \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) elimination or the leading-principal-minor criterion decides positive definiteness with polynomial bit complexity. This also decides the stable-reference promise in \(\mathcal R_q\).

Now guess a canonical encoding of a permutation \(\pi\). Verify that it is a bijection, check each rational denominator \(d_{\pi,i}\neq0\), construct \(B_\pi\) by the normalized-candidate definition, and apply (3) with \(C=B_\pi\). All arithmetic has polynomial bit complexity because normalization performs only rational division on input entries. Exactly one witness is accepted for each member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)\), and no other witness is accepted. Therefore the extended count, and hence its restriction to \(\mathcal R_q\), belongs to \(\#\mathrm P\).

For hardness, the stable-orbit realization theorem is a deterministic polynomial-time map from a simple graph \(G\) to a matrix \(W_G\in\mathcal R_{3n}\), and it gives the exact equality
\[
 N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W_G)=|\mathcal I(G)|. \tag{4}
\]
The independent-set counting lemma is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions. Equation (4) is a single, count-preserving oracle call, so computing \(N_{\mathrm{stab}}\) on \(\mathcal R_q\) is \(\#\mathrm P\)-hard under those reductions. Together with membership, this proves \(\#\mathrm P\)-completeness.

If an FPRAS existed on the images \(W_G\) of graphs of maximum degree six, applying it after the same map and using (4) would preserve both relative error and success probability, yielding an FPRAS for independent-set counting on maximum-degree-six graphs. This contradicts the cited degree-six inapproximability theorem unless \(\mathrm{RP}=\mathrm{NP}\). There is no subtraction, interpolation, or approximation-sensitive postprocessing in this transfer.

Finally define the zero-one support matrix
\[
 A(W)_{ri}=\mathbf1\{W_{ri}\neq0\}.
\]
By the admissible-orbit definition, a permutation \(\pi\) is admissible exactly when
\(\prod_iA(W)_{\pi(i),i}=1\). Therefore
\[
 N_{\mathrm{adm}}(W)
 =\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_q}\prod_{i=1}^qA(W)_{\pi(i),i}
 =\operatorname{per}(A(W)).
\]
The support matrix is nonnegative, so the cited permanent theorem supplies an FPRAS. This proves the claimed separation between the unfiltered assignment orbit and its Schur-stable suborbit.

theorem.statement:
For every simple graph \(G\) on \(n\geq1\) vertices and every \(S\subseteq V\), the exact-pencil handle is valid for the graph gadget. Writing \(T=V\setminus S\), \(a=16/25\), \(h_0(z)=z^2-p-r\), \(h_1(z)=z^3+az-ar\), \(c_i=a\) on \(S\), and \(c_i=1\) on \(T\), one has the polynomial identity
\[
 \det(zI_{3n}-B_{\pi_S})
 =z^{,n-|S|}\det\!\left(
   \operatorname{diag}(h_1(z)I_S,h_0(z)I_T)
   -zg\operatorname{diag}(c_i)A_G\right).
\]
On each critical disk centered at \(\zeta_\pm=(-3\pm\mathrm i\sqrt{91})/10\) with radius \(1/16\), the \(T\)-block Schur complement has no pole. The scalar coordinate \(f_\delta(z)=h_1(z)/(az)\) has, for every \(|y|\leq1/8\), a unique analytic inverse \(z=z_{\delta,\pm}(y)\) in the corresponding disk, with nonzero derivative. Under \(y=gw\), analytic zero multiplicities are preserved and the critical determinant is
\[
 \det\!\left(wI_S-A_G[S,S]-E(z_{\delta,\pm}(gw))\right),
 \qquad \|E(z)\|_2\leq4gn^2.
\]
For a suitable \(t\in[-3/4,-1/2]\), the rectangle \(-n-1<\operatorname{Re}w<t\), \(|\operatorname{Im}w|<1\) contains a zero of this determinant if and only if \(S\notin\mathcal I(G)\). Consequently, every independent intended assignment has all critical roots of modulus at most \(1-\delta/10\), whereas every non-independent intended assignment has a root of modulus at least \(1+g/20\). All its noncritical roots have modulus less than \(9/10\). Finally, an admissible assignment containing a root-only permutation cycle has spectral radius greater than \(1/(2g)\), and an admissible assignment with no root-only cycle but with a local \(u_i\)-\(w_i\) swap has an eigenvalue with real part greater than \(5/4\).
theorem.proof_tex:
Put \(r_0=15/16\), so \(r=r_0(1-\delta)\), and put
\[
 b=-p-r=\frac58+\frac{15}{16}\delta,
 \qquad d_0(z)=\frac{h_0(z)}z=z+\frac bz,
 \qquad f_\delta(z)=\frac{h_1(z)}{az}=\frac{z^2}{a}+1-\frac rz.
\]
We first derive the exact pencil from the normalized-candidate and graph-gadget definitions. If \(i\notin S\), the three eigenvector equations for \(B_{\pi_S}\) are
\[
 zu_i=v_i+w_i+g\sum_j(A_G)_{ij}u_j,
 \qquad zv_i=pu_i,
 \qquad zw_i=ru_i.
\]
Eliminating \(v_i,w_i\) gives
\[
 h_0(z)u_i=zg\sum_j(A_G)_{ij}u_j.
\]
If \(i\in S\), row normalization uses \(W_G[v_i,u_i]=-p\), and the equations are
\[
 zu_i=p^{-1}v_i,
 \qquad zv_i=u_i-w_i-g\sum_j(A_G)_{ij}u_j,
 \qquad zw_i=ru_i.
\]
Since \(-p^{-1}=a\), elimination gives
\[
 h_1(z)u_i=azg\sum_j(A_G)_{ij}u_j.
\]
Performing these eliminations at determinant level contributes one factor \(z\) for every unswitched vertex and no such factor for a switched vertex. Hence, for \(z\neq0\),
\[
 \det(zI_{3n}-B_{\pi_S})
 =z^{,n-|S|}\det\!\left(
   \operatorname{diag}(h_1(z)I_S,h_0(z)I_T)
   -zg\operatorname{diag}(c_i)A_G\right).
\]
Both sides are monic polynomials of degree \(3n\), so equality away from \(z=0\) extends to the asserted polynomial identity, including all zero multiplicities.

We next certify the Schur complement. On either disk \(|z-\zeta_\pm|\leq1/16\), one has \(|z|\geq15/16\). Since every adjacency submatrix has operator norm at most \(n\),
\[
 |d_0(z)|\geq |z|-\frac b{|z|}
 \geq\frac{13}{48}-\delta,
\]
and therefore
\[
 \sigma_{\min}\!\left(d_0(z)I_T-gA_G[T,T]\right)
 \geq\frac{13}{48}-\delta-gn>\frac14.
\]
Here the last inequality follows from
\[
 \varepsilon_n\leq2^{-44},\qquad
 gn=\frac{n}{2^{80}(n+1)^8}<2^{-80},
 \qquad \delta\leq2^{-132}.
\]
Thus the inverse exists throughout both closed disks and has norm at most \(4\). Dividing the \(S\)-rows by \(az\), the \(T\)-rows by \(z\), and taking the \(T\)-block Schur complement gives
\[
 \Phi_S(z)=f_\delta(z)I_S-gA_G[S,S]
 -g^2A_G[S,T]\bigl(d_0(z)I_T-gA_G[T,T]\bigr)^{-1}A_G[T,S].
\]
With
\[
 E(z)=gA_G[S,T]\bigl(d_0(z)I_T-gA_G[T,T]\bigr)^{-1}A_G[T,S],
\]
the submatrix norm bound and the inverse bound imply
\[
 \|E(z)\|_2\leq4gn^2=:\eta.
\]
This proves the asserted absence of poles uniformly in \(G\) and \(S\).

It remains to justify the inverse coordinate and multiplicity statement. Work first at \(\zeta=\zeta_+\); conjugation gives the other disk. Since \(f_0(\zeta)=0\), direct algebra yields
\[
 F:=f_0'(\zeta)=\frac{3\zeta^2+a}{a\zeta},
 \qquad |F|^2=\frac{3913}{256}>\left(\frac{39}{10}\right)^2.
\]
For \(v=z-\zeta\) with \(|v|\leq1/16\), one has \(|f_0''(z)|<6\); hence
\[
 f_\delta(\zeta+v)=Fv+R_0(v)+\frac{r_0\delta}{\zeta+v},
 \qquad |R_0(v)|\leq3|v|^2.
\]
On \(|v|=1/16\), the linear term is larger than \(39/160\), whereas, for \(|y|\leq1/8\),
\[
 |R_0(v)|+\left|\frac{r_0\delta}{\zeta+v}\right|+|y|
 \leq\frac3{256}+\delta+\frac18<\frac{39}{160}.
\]
The boundary-zero-count lemma applied to the homotopy from \(Fv\) to \(f_\delta(\zeta+v)-y\) shows that the latter has exactly one zero in the disk. Moreover,
\[
 |f_\delta'(\zeta+v)-F|\leq6|v|+2\delta<\frac12<|F|,
\]
so the derivative is nonzero. The unique solution \(z_\delta(y)\) is consequently analytic in \(y\).

The same estimates also give explicit radial control. From the preceding equation and \(|v|\leq1/16\),
\[
 \left(\frac{39}{10}-\frac3{16}\right)|v|\leq |y|+\delta,
 \qquad |v|\leq\frac{|y|+\delta}{3}.
\]
Define
\[
 \beta=F^{-1}=\frac{a\zeta}{3\zeta^2+a},
 \qquad \gamma=-\frac{3/5}{3\zeta^2+a}.
\]
Rearranging the scalar equation and using \(|\beta|<1/3\) gives
\[
 |z_\delta(y)-\zeta-\beta y-\gamma\delta|
 \leq(|y|+\delta)^2.
\]
The exact coefficients satisfy
\[
 \operatorname{Re}(\overline\zeta\beta)=-\frac8{43},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Im}(\overline\zeta\beta)=\frac{72\sqrt{91}}{3913},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Re}(\overline\zeta\gamma)=-\frac9{43}.
\]
Since
\[
 \bigl||\zeta+v|-1-\operatorname{Re}(\overline\zeta v)\bigr|
 \leq |v|^2,
\]
we obtain the disk-uniform expansion
\[
 |z_\delta(y)|=1-\frac9{43}\delta
 +\operatorname{Re}\!\left[
   \left(-\frac8{43}+\mathrm i\frac{72\sqrt{91}}{3913}\right)y\right]+R,
 \qquad |R|\leq4(|y|+\delta)^2. \tag{1}
\]

If \(z\) is a critical zero of \(\det\Phi_S\), a unit nullvector and the displayed inverse bound give
\[
 |f_\delta(z)|\leq gn+4g^2n^2<\frac18.
\]
Writing \(f_\delta(z)=gw\), uniqueness of the inverse coordinate gives \(z=z_\delta(gw)\), and
\[
 \Phi_S(z)=g\left(wI_S-A_G[S,S]-E(z_\delta(gw))\right). \tag{2}
\]
Because \(f_\delta'(z)\neq0\), the map \(w\mapsto z_\delta(gw)\) is locally biholomorphic. The eliminated \(T\)-block determinant and all row-scaling factors are nonzero on the critical disk. Equation (2), with its nonzero scalar factor \(g^{|S|}\), therefore proves equality of the zero order of the full characteristic polynomial in \(z\) and the zero order of the displayed determinant in \(w\). Thus multiplicities are preserved rather than merely counted setwise.

We now perform the negative-mode homotopy. If \(S\notin\mathcal I(G)\), choose an edge \(ij\) in \(G[S]\). The unit vector \((e_i-e_j)/\sqrt2\) has Rayleigh quotient \(-1\), so
\[
 \lambda_{\min}(A_G[S,S])\leq-1.
\]
Among the at most \(n\) real eigenvalues, choose
\(t\in[-3/4,-1/2]\) at distance at least \(1/[8(n+1)]\) from all of them: the eigenvalues divide this interval of length \(1/4\) into at most \(n+1\) gaps, and the midpoint of a largest gap has the stated separation. On the boundary of
\[
 \mathcal Q_t=\{w:-n-1<\operatorname{Re}w<t,\ |\operatorname{Im}w|<1\},
\]
normality of the real symmetric adjacency matrix gives
\[
 \left\|(wI_S-A_G[S,S])^{-1}\right\|_2\leq8(n+1).
\]
Indeed the right side of the rectangle has the chosen spectral separation, the horizontal sides have imaginary part of magnitude one, and the left side is at distance at least two because \(\|A_G[S,S]\|_2\leq n-1\). Hence
\[
 8(n+1)\eta=32gn^2(n+1)<1.
\]
The pencils
\[
 wI_S-A_G[S,S]-sE(z_\delta(gw)),\qquad 0\leq s\leq1,
\]
are therefore nonsingular on \(\partial\mathcal Q_t\). They are analytic there because \(|gw|<1/8\) on the closed rectangle and the already proved Schur denominator never vanishes. The boundary-zero-count lemma now preserves the number of zeros with multiplicity. At \(s=0\), the eigenvalue \(\lambda_{\min}(A_G[S,S])\) lies in \(\mathcal Q_t\), so at \(s=1\) at least one zero persists. Conversely, if \(S\in\mathcal I(G)\), then \(A_G[S,S]=0\), and a unit nullvector at any zero of (2) gives \(|w|\leq\eta<1/2\); thus no such zero lies in \(\mathcal Q_t\). This proves the claimed if and only if.

At any retained zero, the same unit-nullvector argument and normality give
\[
 \operatorname{dist}\!\left(w,\operatorname{spec}(A_G[S,S])\right)\leq\eta,
 \quad |\operatorname{Im}w|\leq\eta,
 \quad \operatorname{Re}w<t\leq-\frac12,
 \quad |w|\leq2(n+1).
\]
Since \(72\sqrt{91}/3913<1/5\), applying (1) with \(y=gw\) yields
\[
 |z|\geq1+\frac4{43}g-\frac9{43}\delta
 -g\eta-4\bigl(2g(n+1)+\delta\bigr)^2.
\]
Using \(\delta/g=\varepsilon_n\leq2^{-44}\) and
\(g(n+1)^2\leq2^{-86}\), the total subtracted quantity after the leading \(4g/43\) is less than \((4/43-1/20)g\). Thus \(|z|\geq1+g/20\). If \(S\in\mathcal I(G)\), then \(|w|\leq\eta\), so \(|y|\leq4g^2n^2\), and (1), together with
\[
 \frac{g^2n^2}{\delta}=\varepsilon_n n^2\leq2^{-44},
\]
gives \(|z|\leq1-\delta/10\). The conjugate disk has the same bounds.

For completeness, we locate every noncritical root. At \(g=\delta=0\), an unswitched vertex has characteristic polynomial
\[
 z\left(z^2+\frac58\right),
\]
and a switched vertex has characteristic polynomial
\[
 (z-3/5)(z-\zeta_+)(z-\zeta_-).
\]
On the three contours \(|z|=9/10\) and \(|z-\zeta_\pm|=1/16\), direct root-distance products bound each relevant local determinant below by \(3/1000\). Every \(2\)-by-\(2\) cofactor of the local resolvents has modulus at most \(8\), hence every local adjugate has operator norm at most \(24\), and the block-diagonal resolvent norm is less than \(8192\). Changing \(\delta\) and adding the graph coupling changes the block diagonal matrix by operator norm at most \(2\delta+gn\), while
\[
 8192(2\delta+gn)<1.
\]
The boundary-zero-count lemma therefore shows that exactly \(3n-2|S|\) roots lie in \(|z|<9/10\) and exactly \(|S|\) roots lie in each critical disk. These counts sum to \(3n\), so no root is omitted.

It remains to exclude unintended admissible assignments. A nontrivial permutation cycle follows a nonzero off-diagonal entry of \(W_G\). Since each leaf \(v_i\) or \(w_i\) has only its root \(u_i\) as an off-diagonal neighbor, a cycle containing a leaf must be the corresponding two-cycle. Every admissible permutation is therefore a disjoint union of fixed points, local \(u_i\)-\(v_i\) swaps, local \(u_i\)-\(w_i\) swaps, and cycles using roots only.

Suppose first that a nonempty set \(C\) of roots belongs to root-only cycles. After putting those roots first,
\[
 B_\pi=g^{-1}H+E_0,
 \qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}P&R\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(P\) is the permutation matrix of the root cycles and each row of \(R\) has the two entries \(-1\) at the leaves of the selected original root. Directly from the normalized rows, the remaining entries have modulus at most \(2\), and counting their supports gives \(\|E_0\|_2\leq\|E_0\|_{\mathrm F}\leq6n\). Since \(\|P^{-1}R\|_2=\sqrt2\), the shear
\[
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}I&-P^{-1}R\\0&I\end{pmatrix}
\]
satisfies
\[
 Q^{-1}HQ=\operatorname{diag}(P,0),
 \qquad \|Q\|_2\|Q^{-1}\|_2<6.
\]
Consequently
\[
 Q^{-1}(gB_\pi)Q=\operatorname{diag}(P,0)+F_0,
 \qquad \|F_0\|_2<36gn.
\]
On \(|z|=1/2\), the normal matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(P,0)\) has resolvent norm at most \(2\); because \(72gn<1\), the straight-line perturbation is boundary-invertible. The boundary-zero-count lemma preserves the \(|C|\) eigenvalues outside that circle. Hence \(\rho(B_\pi)>1/(2g)\).

Finally suppose there is no root-only cycle but some \(u_i\)-\(w_i\) swap. At zero graph coupling the possible local blocks are
\[
 M_0(\delta)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\p&0&0\\r&0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 M_1(\delta)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/p&0\\1&0&-1\\r&0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 M_2(\delta)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1/r\\p&0&0\\1&-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
At \(\delta=0\), their characteristic polynomials are, respectively,
\[
 z(z^2+5/8),\qquad
 (z-3/5)(z^2+(3/5)z+1),\qquad
 z^3-(16/15)z-5/3.
\]
The last polynomial has one real root in \((7/5,3/2)\), and its other two roots have real part less than \(-7/10\). On \(|z-3/2|=1/4\), its determinant modulus is greater than
\[
 \frac3{20}\left(\frac{39}{20}\right)^2>\frac12,
\]
whereas the first two polynomials have no zero in the disk. Every local adjugate on the contour has norm at most \(24\), so every local resolvent has norm at most \(64\). The combined change due to \(\delta\) and graph coupling has norm at most \(2\delta+gn\), and \(64(2\delta+gn)<1\). The boundary-zero-count lemma preserves one eigenvalue in this disk for every \(M_2\) block. Every point of the disk has real part greater than \(5/4\). Thus every such assignment is unstable. This completes the uniform no-pole, multiplicity, negative-mode, and unintended-assignment certification.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(D\subset\mathbb C\) be a bounded simply connected domain with piecewise \(C^1\) boundary, and let \(F:[0,1]\times\overline D\to\mathbb C\) be continuous, continuously differentiable in the homotopy parameter, and holomorphic in a neighborhood of \(\overline D\) in its second argument. If \(F(t,z)\neq0\) for every \((t,z)\in[0,1]\times\partial D\), then the number of zeros of \(F(t,\cdot)\) in \(D\), counted with analytic multiplicity, is independent of \(t\). The same conclusion applies to \(F(t,z)=\det M_t(z)\) for a square analytic matrix pencil that is nonsingular on \(\partial D\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix a positively oriented parametrization of \(\partial D\). Since the boundary is compact and \(F\) is nonzero there, the logarithmic-derivative integral
\[
 N(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm i}\int_{\partial D}
       \frac{\partial_zF(t,z)}{F(t,z)}\,dz
\]
is well defined and continuous in \(t\). For a fixed \(t\), factor \(F(t,z)=(z-z_0)^mG(z)\) in a small disk about each zero \(z_0\), where \(G(z_0)\neq0\). Integration of the logarithmic derivative around the small disk gives \(m\): the term \(m/(z-z_0)\) integrates to \(2\pi\mathrm i m\), while the integral of \(G'/G\) is zero because a nonvanishing holomorphic function on a disk has a holomorphic logarithm, obtained by integrating \(G'/G\) from the center. Deforming \(\partial D\) to the disjoint union of these small circles therefore shows that \(N(t)\) is exactly the sum of the zero multiplicities in \(D\). In particular, \(N(t)\) is integer valued. A continuous integer-valued function on \([0,1]\) is constant, proving the first assertion. For an analytic matrix pencil, its determinant is holomorphic, is nonzero exactly when the pencil is nonsingular, and its analytic zero order is the algebraic multiplicity used in the claim; applying the scalar conclusion proves the last assertion.

added_lemmas.statement: Valiant's counting problem \(\mathrm{MONOTONE\ 2\mbox{-}SAT}\), which asks for the number of satisfying assignments of a conjunction of positive two-variable clauses, is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete under polynomial-time oracle reductions.

added_lemmas.statement: The function \(G\mapsto|\mathcal I(G)|\), the number of independent sets of a finite simple graph, is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions.
added_lemmas.proof_tex: Membership in \(\#\mathrm P\) is immediate: a vertex subset is a polynomial-size witness, and every edge can be checked in polynomial time. For hardness, start with an instance of Valiant's \(\mathrm{MONOTONE\ 2\mbox{-}SAT}\) problem. A clause of the form \(x_i\vee x_i\) forces \(x_i=1\); set every such variable to one and delete all clauses thereby satisfied. This preserves the number of satisfying assignments because each forced variable has exactly one possible value. Delete duplicate remaining clauses, and form the simple graph with one vertex per remaining variable and edge \(ij\) for the clause \(x_i\vee x_j\). A truth assignment satisfies all clauses exactly when its set of true variables is a vertex cover. Complementation is a bijection from vertex covers to independent sets, including arbitrary choices of isolated vertices. If preprocessing removes every variable, the answer is the directly computable value one; otherwise the graph is nonempty. Thus this is a polynomial-time count-preserving Turing reduction. Composing it with the cited \(\#\mathrm P\)-completeness of \(\mathrm{MONOTONE\ 2\mbox{-}SAT}\) proves \(\#\mathrm P\)-hardness under polynomial-time Turing reductions.

proofs.proof_tex:
Let \((P_X,W,e)\in\mathcal M_q\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:invertible\mbox{-}equations}\) and the structural equation give the square mixing representation
\[
 X=Ae,\qquad A=W^{-1}.
\]
The coordinates of \(e\) are mutually independent by assumption \(\mathrm{ass:independent\mbox{-}errors}\), have positive finite variances by assumption \(\mathrm{ass:nonzero\mbox{-}error\mbox{-}variances}\), and at most one is Gaussian by assumption \(\mathrm{ass:non\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}errors}\). The cited square-ICA identification lemma therefore implies that \(P_X\) determines \([W]_{\mathrm{mon}}\). This is identification of a structural orbit from the observed law; it does not define the orbit to equal an observed functional.

It remains to prove that the count does not depend on the representative of this identified orbit. Let
\[
 \widetilde W=MW,
 \qquad
 M=D P_\sigma,
 \qquad
 D=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_q),
 \qquad a_i\neq0,
\]
where \(\sigma\in\mathfrak S_q\). For \(\pi\in\mathfrak S_q\), define \(\tau=\sigma\circ\pi\). By the convention \((P_\pi)_{ij}=\mathbf 1\{j=\pi(i)\}\), the \(i\)-th row of \(P_\pi D P_\sigma W\) is \(a_{\pi(i)}\) times row \(\sigma(\pi(i))\) of \(W\). Hence
\[
 \widetilde W_{\pi(i),i}
 =a_{\pi(i)}W_{\sigma(\pi(i)),i}
 =a_{\pi(i)}W_{\tau(i),i}.
\]
Because every \(a_{\pi(i)}\) is nonzero, this proves the equivalence
\[
 \pi\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{adm}}(\widetilde W)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \tau\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{adm}}(W).
\]
The map \(\pi\mapsto\sigma\circ\pi\) is a bijection of \(\mathfrak S_q\), with inverse \(\tau\mapsto\sigma^{-1}\circ\tau\), so it is a bijection of the two admissible sets.

For an admissible \(\pi\), direct substitution into the normalization gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \widetilde W_\pi
 &=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(
      \frac{1}{a_{\pi(i)}W_{\tau(i),i}}:i\in[q]
    \right)P_\pi D P_\sigma W\\
 &=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(
      \frac{1}{W_{\tau(i),i}}:i\in[q]
    \right)P_\tau W
 =W_\tau.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(I_q-\widetilde W_\pi=I_q-W_\tau\), and so
\[
 \rho(I_q-\widetilde W_\pi)<1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \rho(I_q-W_\tau)<1.
\]
The admissible-set bijection consequently restricts to a bijection
\[
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(\widetilde W)
 \longleftrightarrow
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)
\]
that preserves the normalized coefficient matrix itself. Taking finite cardinalities yields
\[
 N_{\mathrm{stab}}(\widetilde W)=N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W).
\]
Thus the explicitly identified map is
\[
 P_X\longmapsto[W]_{\mathrm{mon}}
       \longmapsto N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W),
\]
and the second arrow is well defined by the proved representative invariance.

Fix one law in \(\mathcal M_q^{\mathrm{FOBI}}\). All constants below may depend on this law. With the corrected central-moment definition of \(\kappa\), put
\[
 \mu_e=\mathbb E[e],
 \qquad
 \sigma_i^2=\operatorname{Var}(e_i),
 \qquad
 D=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_q),
 \qquad
 \xi=D^{-1}(e-\mu_e).
\]
The nonzero-variance assumption makes every division by \(\sigma_i\) valid. Independence of the coordinates of \(e\) gives independence of the coordinates of \(\xi\), and
\[
 \mathbb E[\xi]=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[\xi\xi^{\mathsf T}]=I_q,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[\xi_i^4]-3=\kappa_i.
\]
Moreover \(e=WX\), so \(\|e\|_2\leq\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|X\|_2\). The finite eighth-moment assumption therefore implies \(\mathbb E\|\xi\|_2^8<\infty\). Centering the structural equation yields
\[
 X-\mathbb E[X]=\Omega\xi,
 \qquad
 \Omega=W^{-1}D.
\]
Both \(W\) and \(D\) are nonsingular, and hence
\[
 \Sigma:=\operatorname{Var}(X)=\Omega\Omega^{\mathsf T}\succ0.
\]
This establishes the positivity needed for whitening. We will repeatedly use the following elementary iid averaging argument. If \(h(X)\) is integrable, put \(h_K=h\mathbf 1\{|h|\leq K\}\). Chebyshev's inequality gives
\[
 \Pr\!\left(
  \left|m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m(h_K(X_j)-\mathbb E[h_K(X)])\right|>\varepsilon
 \right)
 \leq\frac{K^2}{m\varepsilon^2}.
\]
Markov's inequality gives
\[
 \Pr\!\left(
  m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m|h(X_j)-h_K(X_j)|>\varepsilon
 \right)
 \leq\frac{\mathbb E|h(X)-h_K(X)|}{\varepsilon}.
\]
The expectation on the right tends to zero as \(K\to\infty\). Taking \(K\to\infty\) after \(m\to\infty\), and using \(|\mathbb E[h-h_K]|\leq\mathbb E|h-h_K|\), proves
\[
 m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m h(X_j)\longrightarrow_{\Pr}\mathbb E[h(X)].
\]
Apply this result to the coordinate functions \(X_a\) and \(X_aX_b\), which are integrable under the eighth-moment condition. The algebraic identity expressing sample covariance through empirical first and second raw moments then gives \(\widehat\Sigma_m\to_{\Pr}\Sigma\). Consequently \(\Pr(\widehat\Sigma_m\succ0)\to1\), so the fallback branch in the estimator definition has asymptotically vanishing probability.

The population whitening calculation also verifies the FOBI rank condition explicitly. Set
\[
 H=\Sigma^{-1/2}\Omega,
 \qquad
 Y=\Sigma^{-1/2}(X-\mathbb E[X])=H\xi.
\]
Since \(HH^{\mathsf T}=I_q\), the square matrix \(H\) is orthogonal. Independence and centering give, for \(i\neq j\),
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[\|\xi\|_2^2\xi_i\xi_j\right]=0,
\]
whereas
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[\|\xi\|_2^2\xi_i^2\right]
 =\mathbb E[\xi_i^4]+
   \sum_{k\neq i}\mathbb E[\xi_i^2]\mathbb E[\xi_k^2]
 =\kappa_i+q+2.
\]
It follows that the population FOBI matrix is
\[
 F:=\mathbb E[\|Y\|_2^2YY^{\mathsf T}]
 =H\operatorname{diag}(\kappa_1+q+2,\ldots,\kappa_q+q+2)H^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The pairwise-distinct-kurtosis assumption makes all eigenvalues in this display simple. Thus all inverse eigengaps used below are nonzero. If \(O_0\) is the population eigenvector matrix in decreasing-eigenvalue order, then for some permutation matrix \(P\) and sign matrix \(J\),
\[
 O_0=HPJ,
 \qquad
 A_0:=O_0^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1/2}
 =JP^{\mathsf T}\Omega^{-1}
 =JP^{\mathsf T}D^{-1}W.
\]
Hence \(A_0\in[W]_{\mathrm{mon}}\), and its row-normalization
\[
 U_0:=\ell(A_0)
\]
belongs to \(\mathcal O_U(W)\).

By the cited FOBI pointwise-limit lemma, the empirical eigenvectors can be aligned with this population chart by signed row permutations. Thus there are signed permutation matrices \(H_m\) and their induced orthogonal vectorization actions
\[
 Q_m\operatorname{vec}(A)=\operatorname{vec}(H_mA),
 \qquad Q_m\in\mathcal H_q,
\]
such that, with \(\overline A_m=H_m\widehat A_m^{\mathrm F}\),
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vec}(\overline A_m-A_0)
 =m^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_A(X_j)+o_{\Pr}(1).
\]
For a matrix \(A\) with nonzero rows, the row-normalization map is differentiable, with rowwise differential
\[
 \bigl(D\ell_A[H]\bigr)_{i\boldsymbol\cdot}
 =\frac{H_{i\boldsymbol\cdot}}{\|A_{i\boldsymbol\cdot}\|_2}
 -\frac{A_{i\boldsymbol\cdot}H_{i\boldsymbol\cdot}^{\mathsf T}}
  {\|A_{i\boldsymbol\cdot}\|_2^3}A_{i\boldsymbol\cdot}.
\]
Every row of the nonsingular matrix \(A_0\) is nonzero, so Taylor expansion of this displayed formula gives
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vec}(H_m\widehat U_m-U_0)
 =m^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_{\mathrm F}(X_j;P_X)+o_{\Pr}(1)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ Z,
 \qquad
 Z\sim N(0,V_{\mathrm{FOBI}}).
\]
This derives the normalized-row limit from the cited unmixing limit rather than assuming it. In particular,
\[
 \|H_m\widehat U_m-U_0\|_{\mathrm F}=O_{\Pr}(m^{-1/2}).
\]

We next prove covariance consistency, including the plug-in step. In a neighborhood of the fixed law on which \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)>0\) and all kurtosis gaps are bounded away from zero, the FOBI influence function is a polynomial of degree at most four in the centered observation whose coefficients are continuous functions of the mean, covariance, fourth moments, and simple eigensystem. Apply the iid averaging argument above to every monomial of degree at most four; its integrability follows from the eighth-moment condition. The empirical counterparts of all those coefficients therefore converge in probability by continuity of inversion, the positive-definite square root, and simple-eigenvalue projectors. Hence, on events whose probabilities tend to one, there is a random \(a_m\to_{\Pr}0\) such that
\[
 \|Q_m\widehat\psi_{m,j}-\psi_{\mathrm F}(X_j;P_X)\|_2
 \leq a_m(1+\|X_j\|_2^4)
 \qquad(1\leq j\leq m).
\]
The eighth-moment assumption and Markov's inequality imply
\[
 \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m
 \|Q_m\widehat\psi_{m,j}-\psi_{\mathrm F}(X_j;P_X)\|_2^2
 \leq
 a_m^2\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m(1+\|X_j\|_2^4)^2
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}0.
\]
Indeed, the sample average on the right is \(O_{\Pr}(1)\), because its expectation is the fixed finite number \(\mathbb E[(1+\|X\|_2^4)^2]\). Since the influence function has mean zero and finite second moment, apply the proved iid averaging result to each integrable product of two influence coordinates, and use Cauchy--Schwarz for the plug-in cross terms. This gives
\[
 Q_m\widehat V_mQ_m^{\mathsf T}
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}
 \mathbb E[\psi_{\mathrm F}(X;P_X)\psi_{\mathrm F}(X;P_X)^{\mathsf T}]
 =V_{\mathrm{FOBI}}.
\]
Because \(Q_m\in\mathcal H_q\) and this finite group is closed under transposition, the last display is equivalent to
\[
 \min_{Q\in\mathcal H_q}
 \|\widehat V_m-QV_{\mathrm{FOBI}}Q^{\mathsf T}\|_{\mathrm F}
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}0.
\]

For the Gaussian-radius calibration, first suppose \(q\geq2\). The limiting covariance is not the zero matrix. Indeed, at standardized independent components, Theorem 8's off-diagonal influence coordinates are, for \(k\neq l\),
\[
 \phi_{kl}(\xi)
 =\frac{
 (\xi_k^3-\gamma_k)\xi_l+(\xi_l^3-\gamma_l)\xi_k
 +\sum_{s\neq k,l}\xi_s^2\xi_k\xi_l
 -(\kappa_k+q+4)\xi_k\xi_l
 }{\kappa_k-\kappa_l},
 \qquad
 \gamma_k=\mathbb E[\xi_k^3].
\]
Each coordinate has mean zero, and direct subtraction gives
\[
 \phi_{lk}(\xi)=-\phi_{kl}(\xi)-\xi_k\xi_l.
\]
If both variances were zero, both mean-zero variables would vanish almost surely, forcing \(\xi_k\xi_l=0\) almost surely. This contradicts independence and unit variances, because
\[
 \mathbb E[\xi_k^2\xi_l^2]
 =\mathbb E[\xi_k^2]\mathbb E[\xi_l^2]=1.
\]
The differential of row normalization removes only the radial diagonal coordinate at the identity chart and retains these off-diagonal coordinates. Hence \(V_{\mathrm{FOBI}}\neq0\).

Let \(c_{1-\alpha}\) be the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\|Z\|_2\) for \(Z\sim N(0,V_{\mathrm{FOBI}})\). A nonzero positive-semidefinite Gaussian covariance has at least one positive eigenvalue, so \(\|Z\|_2\) has a continuous distribution, with no atom at \(c_{1-\alpha}>0\). Conditional on the sample, multiplication of \(Z_m^*\) by \(Q_m\) preserves its Euclidean norm and changes its covariance to \(Q_m\widehat V_mQ_m^{\mathsf T}\). Continuity of the positive-semidefinite square root and the proved covariance convergence therefore give
\[
 c_{m,1-\alpha}\longrightarrow_{\Pr}c_{1-\alpha}.
\]
Combining this with the normalized-row limit and the absence of a boundary atom yields
\[
 \Pr\!\left{
  \sqrt m\,\|H_m\widehat U_m-U_0\|_{\mathrm F}
  \leq c_{m,1-\alpha}
 \right}
 \longrightarrow 1-\alpha.
\]

On the event in braces, set \(R_m=H_m^{\mathsf T}U_0\). Signed row permutations preserve \(\mathcal U_q\), so \(R_m\in\mathcal O_U(W)\), and orthogonality gives
\[
 \sqrt m\,\|R_m-\widehat U_m\|_{\mathrm F}
 =\sqrt m\,\|U_0-H_m\widehat U_m\|_{\mathrm F}
 \leq c_{m,1-\alpha}.
\]
Thus \(R_m\in\mathcal E_m\). By symmetrization, \(K_m\) then contains the entire normalized monomial orbit of \(R_m\), which equals \(\mathcal O_U(W)\). In particular \(\ell(W)\in K_m\). The matrix \(\ell(W)\) is invertible because it is obtained from the invertible \(W\) by nonzero row scaling. The proved representative invariance gives
\[
 N_{\mathrm{stab}}(\ell(W))=N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W).
\]
By the definition of the confidence image, the preceding inclusions imply
\[
 \left\{
  \sqrt m\,\|H_m\widehat U_m-U_0\|_{\mathrm F}
  \leq c_{m,1-\alpha}
 \right\}
 \subseteq
 \{N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)\in C_m^N\}.
\]
Taking lower limits proves
\[
 \liminf_{m\to\infty}
 \Pr\{N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)\in C_m^N\}\geq1-\alpha.
\]
Notice that this is set inversion: it uses no continuity of the integer-valued count.

It remains to prove contraction of the whole random set. Write
\[
 r_m=\frac{c_{m,1-\alpha}}{\sqrt m},
 \qquad
 d_m=\|\widehat U_m-R_m\|_{\mathrm F}.
\]
The covariance convergence makes \(c_{m,1-\alpha}=O_{\Pr}(1)\), while the normalized-row limit gives \(d_m=O_{\Pr}(m^{-1/2})\). Each element of \(\mathcal E_m\) lies within \(r_m\) of \(\widehat U_m\). Signed row permutations act isometrically, so each element of \(K_m\) lies within \(r_m+d_m\) of the corresponding image of \(R_m\), which belongs to \(\mathcal O_U(W)\). Conversely, \(\widehat U_m\in\mathcal E_m\), and every point of \(\mathcal O_U(W)\) is an image of \(R_m\); the corresponding image of \(\widehat U_m\) belongs to \(K_m\) and is within \(d_m\). Therefore
\[
 d_{\mathrm H,F}(K_m,\mathcal O_U(W))
 \leq r_m+d_m
 =O_{\Pr}(m^{-1/2}).
\]
The same alignment gives directly
\[
 d_{\mathrm{orb}}(\widehat A_m^{\mathrm F},W)
 \leq\|\widehat U_m-R_m\|_{\mathrm F}
 =O_{\Pr}(m^{-1/2}).
\]

If \(q=1\), assumption \(W_{11}=1\) gives \(W=(1)\) and \(\mathcal O_U(W)=\{-1,1\}\). Row normalization in one dimension is locally constant, its differential and \(V_{\mathrm{FOBI}}\) are zero, and \(\widehat U_m\in\{-1,1\}\) on both branches of its definition. Hence \(\widehat V_m=0\), \(c_{m,1-\alpha}=0\), and symmetrization gives \(K_m=\{-1,1\}\) exactly. All three conclusions follow with probability one.

Finally, every use of a covariance eigenvalue, a kurtosis gap, and an eighth-moment envelope above concerns the one fixed law. The coverage event only inserts a true orbit representative into \(K_m\); it neither selects a support nor requires normalization denominators to stay uniformly away from zero, and it never invokes local constancy across the unit-circle stability boundary. This proves precisely the stated pointwise, orbit-honest scope.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(W\in\mathcal R_q\), and let \(D(B)\) be the directed support graph having an arrow \(j\to i\) exactly when \(B_{ij}\neq 0\). By \(B=I_q-W\) and assumption \(\mathrm{ass:unit\mbox{-}diagonal}\), for distinct \(i,r\in[q]\) one has
\[
 W_{ri}\neq 0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 B_{ri}=-W_{ri}\neq 0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 i\to r\text{ is an arrow of }D(B).
\]
Let \(\pi\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{adm}}(W)\). Thus \(W_{\pi(i),i}\neq0\) for every \(i\). Write a nontrivial cycle of \(\pi\) as
\[
 i_0\mapsto i_1\mapsto\cdots\mapsto i_{s-1}\mapsto i_0.
\]
The preceding equivalence gives the directed cycle
\[
 i_0\to i_1\to\cdots\to i_{s-1}\to i_0
\]
in \(D(B)\). Hence all vertices of that permutation cycle lie in one strongly connected component. Trivial permutation cycles also lie in one component. It follows that
\[
 \pi(C)=C\qquad\text{for every }C\in\operatorname{SCC}(B).
\]
Consequently restriction defines a map
\[
 R:\mathcal P_{\mathrm{adm}}(W)
 \longrightarrow
 \prod_{C\in\operatorname{SCC}(B)}\mathcal P_{\mathrm{adm}}(W_C),
 \qquad
 R(\pi)=(\pi|_C)_C.
\]
For each component \(C\), the local diagonal normalizer uses precisely the entries \(W_{\pi(i),i}\) with \(i\in C\); these are the same entries in \(W_C\). Thus every restriction is locally admissible. Conversely, given locally admissible permutations \((\sigma_C)_C\), their concatenation \(\sigma\), taken in a fixed topological order of the condensation graph, is a permutation of \([q]\) satisfying
\[
 W_{\sigma(i),i}=(W_C)_{\sigma_C(i),i}\neq0
 \qquad(i\in C).
\]
It is therefore globally admissible. Restriction and concatenation are inverse, so \(R\) is a bijection on admissible fibers.

It remains to identify the stability filter. Put the SCCs in a topological order. The matrices \(B\) and \(W=I_q-B\) are block triangular in this order. Since every admissible \(\pi\) preserves every component, both \(P_\pi\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(d_{\pi,1}^{-1},\ldots,d_{\pi,q}^{-1})\) are block diagonal. Hence
\[
 W_\pi=T_\pi W
\]
is block triangular, and its diagonal block indexed by \(C\) is
\[
 (W_\pi)[C,C]
 =T_{\pi|_C}W_C.
\]
Therefore \(B_\pi=I_q-W_\pi\) is block triangular with diagonal blocks
\[
 B^C_{\pi|_C}:=I_{|C|}-T_{\pi|_C}W_C.
\]
Expanding the determinant of a block-triangular matrix along its diagonal blocks gives, for every \(z\in\mathbb C\),
\[
 \det(zI_q-B_\pi)
 =\prod_{C\in\operatorname{SCC}(B)}
   \det\!\left(zI_{|C|}-B^C_{\pi|_C}\right).
\]
Thus the spectrum of \(B_\pi\), including algebraic multiplicities, is the multiset union of the spectra of its diagonal blocks, and consequently
\[
 \rho(B_\pi)<1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \rho\!\left(B^C_{\pi|_C}\right)<1
 \text{ for every }C\in\operatorname{SCC}(B).
\]
By the definitions of the local normalized candidate and the stable orbit, the right-hand side says exactly that \(\pi|_C\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(W_C)\) for every \(C\). The admissible-fiber bijection therefore restricts to
\[
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)
 \cong
 \prod_{C\in\operatorname{SCC}(B)}
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(W_C).
\]
All sets are finite. Taking cardinalities and using \(N_C=N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W_C)\) yields
\[
 N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)
 =\prod_{C\in\operatorname{SCC}(B)}N_C,
\]
as claimed.

Assume \(W\in\mathcal R_q\). Rational equality testing determines the support arrows exactly. Graph search from each vertex determines mutual reachability, and mutual reachability is an equivalence relation whose classes are exactly \(\operatorname{SCC}(B)\); hence the first step of \(\mathsf{Enum}\) computes the required partition exactly in polynomial time. Next note that every principal SCC block is itself a valid rational stable-reference input. Indeed, in a topological SCC order, \(W\) and \(B\) are block triangular. Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass:rational\mbox{-}input}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:unit\mbox{-}diagonal}\) pass to every \(W_C\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:invertible\mbox{-}equations}\) and block-triangular determinant factorization imply
\[
 0\neq\det(W)=\prod_C\det(W_C),
\]
so every \(W_C\) is invertible. Likewise assumption \(\mathrm{ass:stable\mbox{-}reference}\) and block-triangular spectral factorization give \(\rho(B[C,C])<1\). Hence \(W_C\in\mathcal R_{|C|}\).

Fix a component \(C\) of size \(c\). Form the bipartite graph \(H_C\) with a column copy and a row copy of \(C\), putting an edge \((i,r)\) exactly when \((W_C)_{ri}\neq0\). A perfect matching of \(H_C\) is precisely a bijection \(i\mapsto\pi_C(i)\) for which
\[
 (W_C)_{\pi_C(i),i}\neq0\qquad(i\in C),
\]
and hence, by \(\mathrm{def:admissible\mbox{-}orbit}\), is precisely a member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{adm}}(W_C)\).

Here is a canonical implementation of the stated alternating recursion. Order the columns and, within each column, the incident rows. At a prefix assigning the first \(k\) columns injectively, test each available incident row and recurse exactly when the residual bipartite graph has a perfect matching. The feasibility test is exact: repeatedly augment a current matching along an alternating path. If no augmenting path exists before all residual columns are matched, let \(S\) be the residual columns reachable from an unmatched column by alternating paths. Every row neighboring \(S\) is matched back into \(S\), while \(S\) contains the initial unmatched column, so \(|N(S)|<|S|\); an injection matching all columns is then impossible. If an augmenting path exists, flipping its alternating edges increases the matching size by one. Thus at most \(c\) augmentations, each found by a graph search scanning \(O(e_C)\) edges, decide feasibility in \(O(ce_C)\) elementary operations. Moreover, two perfect extensions of the same prefix have symmetric difference equal to a disjoint union of even alternating cycles. The ordered prefix branch selects the first edge on which two such extensions differ, so this recursion is equivalently an exact-once alternating-cycle recursion.

Every perfect matching determines one and only one root-to-leaf sequence of prefix choices, so it is emitted exactly once. Conversely, a leaf is emitted only after every prefix, including the full assignment, passed the extension test, so every emitted leaf is a perfect matching. To bound the recursion tree, associate each feasible prefix with its lexicographically least perfect-matching extension. For a fixed perfect matching there is at most one associated prefix at each of the \(c+1\) depths. Hence there are at most \((c+1)N_{\mathrm{adm}}(W_C)\) feasible prefixes. At most \(c\) candidate children are tested at each such prefix. Using \(e_C\le c^2\), the initial feasibility test and all recursive work are therefore bounded by
\[
 O\!\left(
    \bigl(c^{1/2}e_C+cN_{\mathrm{adm}}(W_C)\bigr)
    \operatorname{poly}(c,L)
 \right).
\]
The displayed polynomial absorbs the factors from at most \(c\) child tests, at most \(c\) augmentations, and exact arithmetic; the initial \(O(ce_C)\) term has the required form because \(ce_C=(c^{1/2}e_C)c^{1/2}\).

For completeness, the stability screening invoked by \(\mathsf{Enum}\) is exact and has polynomial bit complexity. For a locally admissible matching let
\[
 A=I_c-
 \operatorname{diag}\!\left((W_C)_{\pi_C(i),i}^{-1}:i\in C\right)
 P_{\pi_C}W_C.
\]
Every divisor is nonzero by admissibility, so \(A\) is rational and its encoding length is polynomial in \(c\) and \(L\). Consider the rational linear system
\[
 P-A^{\mathsf T}PA=I_c.
\]
If \(\rho(A)<1\), the series
\[
 P=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(A^k)^{\mathsf T}A^k
\]
converges, is positive definite, and solves the system. Its solution is unique: if \(H=A^{\mathsf T}HA\), then
\[
 H=(A^k)^{\mathsf T}HA^k\longrightarrow0,
\]
because \(\rho(A)<1\), whence \(H=0\). The unique solution is rational because it is the solution of a nonsingular rational linear system. Conversely, if a positive-definite \(P\) solves the equation and \(Av=\lambda v\) for a nonzero complex vector \(v\), then
\[
 (1-|\lambda|^2)v^*Pv
 =v^*(P-A^{\mathsf T}PA)v
 =v^*v>0.
\]
Since \(v^*Pv>0\), this forces \(|\lambda|<1\). Thus
\[
 \rho(A)<1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{the Lyapunov system has a positive-definite solution}.
\]
This equivalence also excludes the boundary \(\rho(A)=1\). Fraction-free elimination solves the \(c^2\)-variable rational system. Exact symmetric elimination then writes a positive-definite candidate as \(P=LDL^{\mathsf T}\), where \(L\) is invertible lower triangular and \(D\) is diagonal; the identity \(x^{\mathsf T}Px=(L^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}D(L^{\mathsf T}x)\) shows directly that \(P\) is positive definite exactly when every diagonal pivot in \(D\) is positive. A zero pivot causes rejection and cannot occur for a positive-definite matrix. Clearing denominators and applying the determinant expansion bounds all intermediate integer lengths by a polynomial in \(c\) and \(L\); hence the test takes \(\operatorname{poly}(c,L)\) bit operations. Normalization and screening of all local matchings therefore preserve the preceding output-sensitive bound. Summing it over the SCCs gives exactly the claimed local screening time.

The screening retains each stable local assignment once. By \(\mathrm{thm:scc\mbox{-}factorization}\), restriction and concatenation give a bijection between the Cartesian product of these retained lists and \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)\). A lexicographic mixed-radix counter visits every tuple once; updating the counter takes at most the number of components, and writing the concatenated permutation takes \(q\) entries. Hence, after local screening, each stable assignment is emitted exactly once with \(O(q)\) delay. The screening bound depends on \(N_{\mathrm{adm}}(W_C)\), including rejected matchings, so it makes no polynomial-delay claim in \(N_{\mathrm{stab}}(W)\) alone.
